chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid from Ibn Faddal from Hammad ibn Uthman from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'The testimony of the beggar who asks [while holding out his hand] is not accepted.' Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'Because he is not trusted for his testimony, and that is because if he is given, he is pleased, and if he is denied, he is displeased.'

key_terms.اَلسَّائِلِ: The beggar / the one who asks
key_terms.فِي كَفِّهِ: In his hand (holding out for alms)

ai.seo_question: Why is the testimony of a beggar not accepted in Islamic jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Shaykh al-Tusi cites this chain to establish that a beggar's (*sa'il*) testimony is invalid due to potential bias (*ghurur*) arising from his financial dependence. The Imam explains that his heart is swayed by the outcome of the case—pleased if granted and resentful if denied—thereby compromising his *amanah* (trustworthiness). This ruling highlights the Shia juristic emphasis on psychological impartiality as a prerequisite for valid legal testimony.
